summary: Psalm 47 calls all nations to clap, shout, and sing because God is king over the whole earth. The poem moves from a summons to praise, through God's rule over peoples and Israel's inheritance, to a vision of the peoples' princes gathered under God's exalted reign.
whyItMatters: This psalm gives Book II of Psalms a compact song of worldwide kingship. It joins Israel's particular story with a larger claim that God's rule reaches all nations.

context.author: The heading says, "For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by the sons of Korah." In Psalms, such headings are ancient features of the collection, though their exact force can include authorship, association, dedication, or performance setting.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping community, with the psalm itself summoning "all you nations" to praise God.
context.date: Psalms is an anthology formed over time; this chapter should not be assigned a single secure date from this chapter alone.
context.setting: The poem belongs within Israel's worship poetry and uses public praise language: clapping, shouting, singing, and trumpet sound.
context.literaryForm: A short Hebrew praise psalm centered on God's kingship over Israel and over all the earth.

outline.heading: Summons to all nations
outline.note: The psalm opens by calling all nations to clap and shout to God with triumph.

outline.heading: The great King over all the earth
outline.note: The reason for praise is God's awesome rule, his subduing of peoples, and his choosing of Jacob's inheritance.

outline.heading: God goes up with praise
outline.note: God's ascent is described with shouting and trumpet sound.

outline.heading: Repeated call to sing
outline.note: The congregation is urged again and again to sing praises because God is king of all the earth.

outline.heading: The nations gathered under God
outline.note: The psalm ends with God reigning from his holy throne while the peoples' princes gather and God is greatly exalted.

keyVerses.text: For Yahweh Most High is awesome. He is a great King over all the earth.
keyVerses.why: This gives the central reason for the psalm's worldwide summons to praise.

keyVerses.text: Sing praises to God! Sing praises! Sing praises to our King! Sing praises!
keyVerses.why: The repeated command shows the poem's urgent, public character as a song of praise.

keyVerses.text: For God is the King of all the earth. Sing praises with understanding.
keyVerses.why: This verse ties praise to recognition of God's rule beyond one people or land.

keyVerses.text: The princes of the peoples are gathered together, the people of the God of Abraham. For the shields of the earth belong to God. He is greatly exalted!
keyVerses.why: The closing verse widens the scene to gathered peoples and earthly powers belonging to God.

themes: God as King over all the earth
Public praise with voice and music

questions.question: Who are the "sons of Korah" in the heading?
questions.answer: The psalm's heading associates it with the sons of Korah and with the Chief Musician. Psalm headings can name performers, collections, genres, or associations, but their exact historical force is debated. So the heading is important evidence for how the psalm was transmitted, while not giving a full biography of its makers.

questions.question: Why does the psalm address "all you nations"?
questions.answer: The opening summons is wider than Israel: all nations are told to clap and shout to God. The reason appears in verse 2 and again in verse 7: God is king over all the earth. The chapter does not explain how every nation responds, but it imagines worldwide praise as fitting because God's rule is worldwide.

questions.question: What does "awesome" mean here?
questions.answer: In verse 2, "awesome" describes Yahweh Most High as a great king, not merely as impressive or exciting. The word points to majesty that evokes reverence. The verse connects that awe to God's rule over all the earth.

questions.question: What is difficult about "He subdues nations under us"?
questions.answer: The verse describes God placing nations and peoples beneath the psalm's speaking community. Readers differ on how to read this in relation to worship: some hear a celebration of God's past or hoped-for victory for Israel, while others focus on how the psalm's later verses gather the peoples under God's kingship. The line should be read as ancient royal and communal praise, not as a direct modern policy statement.

questions.question: What is "our inheritance"?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says God chooses "our inheritance" and calls it "the glory of Jacob whom he loved." Within this chapter, that language ties the community's place and identity to God's choice rather than to self-made possession. The verse does not spell out the geography or history behind the phrase.

questions.question: What might "Selah" mean?
questions.answer: "Selah" appears at the end of verse 4. Translations often preserve this Hebrew sound because its exact performance instruction is no longer known. It likely signals something about ancient performance, but readers should not pretend certainty about its precise meaning.

questions.question: What does "God has gone up" describe?
questions.answer: Verse 5 pictures God going up with a shout and Yahweh with trumpet sound. The chapter itself presents this as a public, musical scene of exaltation. Later Christian readers have sometimes connected this verse with ascension language, but the psalm's own wording first belongs to its praise of God's kingship.

questions.question: Why repeat "Sing praises" so many times?
questions.answer: Verse 6 repeats the command in a way suited to spoken or sung worship. The repetition presses the congregation toward active praise rather than quiet observation. Verse 7 adds that the singing should be "with understanding," so the praise is connected to recognizing God's kingship.

questions.question: Who are "the princes of the peoples" and "the shields of the earth"?
questions.answer: Verse 9 pictures the leaders of peoples gathered together and says the shields of the earth belong to God. "Princes" points to rulers or leaders, while "shields" likely represents earthly powers or protectors within the psalm's royal imagery. The point of the verse is that even the world's authorities are gathered under God's exalted rule.

glossary.def: A phrase in the heading that connects the psalm with musical or worship performance, though the exact ancient role is not explained in the chapter.
The group named in the heading of this psalm; the wording associates the poem with them without settling every detail of authorship or performance.
A preserved Hebrew performance marker in verse 4 whose exact instruction is uncertain.
The place from which verse 8 says God sits and reigns over the nations.
